items.title: Claims and Misreadings of a Matched-Pairs Interval for 5K Times
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Interpret the interval in context, and interpret the confidence level.

(b) The coach makes two claims. Claim 1: the program does not change mean 5K time (μ_d = 0). Claim 2: the program improves mean 5K time by at least 2.5 minutes (μ_d ≥ 2.5). For each claim, state whether the interval supports it, and explain.

(c) The coach also says, "95% of runners improved by between 0.37 and 2.33 minutes." Is this a correct use of the interval? Explain.

(d) Suppose the coach had used a random sample of 80 runners instead of 20, and the sample mean difference and standard deviation were the same. How would the width of the 95% interval change? Give an approximate value for the new margin of error.
items.stimulus: A coach recorded the 5K running times of 20 randomly selected runners before and after a 6-week training program. For each runner, the difference (before minus after) in minutes was calculated; positive differences mean the runner got faster. The differences have no strong skewness and no outliers. Using technology, the coach found a 95% confidence interval for the population mean difference μ_d of (0.37, 2.33) minutes.
items.answer:
(a) We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.37 to 2.33 minutes captures the true mean improvement (before minus after) in 5K time for all runners like these after the 6-week program. The confidence level means that if many random samples of the same size were taken, about 95% of the intervals they produce would capture the true mean difference.

(b) Claim 1: 0 is not in the interval (0.37, 2.33), so it is not a plausible value of μ_d, and the interval provides convincing evidence against Claim 1 (the program is associated with a change in mean 5K time). Claim 2: 2.5 is above the interval, so it is not a plausible value and every plausible value is below it; the interval does not support Claim 2.

(c) No. The interval estimates the population mean difference, not the range of individual values, so it does not describe where 95% of individuals fall.

(d) The interval would be narrower. The standard error s/√n would be about half as large because √80 is about twice √20, so the margin of error would be about half of 0.98, roughly 0.47 minutes.

items.title: Is a Matched-Pairs t-Test Appropriate? Background Music and Puzzle Time
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Define the parameter of interest and state the null and alternative hypotheses for the test.

(b) For the appropriate procedure, decide whether its conditions are met. Justify each decision.

(c) A classmate proposes a two-sample t-test that compares the mean time with music and the mean time without music for these students. Is that appropriate? Explain.
items.stimulus: A teacher suspects that background music slows students down on a puzzle task. She randomly selected 15 students from a large school. Each student completed a puzzle once with music and once without music, in a random order, and the teacher recorded each student's difference (time without music minus time with music) in seconds. The sample of 15 differences has mean −9.3 seconds and standard deviation 12.1 seconds. A dotplot of the 15 differences is strongly right-skewed with one outlier.
items.answer:
(a) Μ_d is the true mean difference (time without music minus time with music), in seconds, for all students at this school. H₀: μ_d = 0 versus Hₐ: μ_d < 0.

(b) The procedure is a one-sample t-test for a population mean difference (matched pairs), applied to the 15 differences. Randomization: the 15 students were randomly selected. 10% condition: 15 students are less than 10% of the students at the school. Sample-data condition: the sample of differences has n = 15, which is less than 30, and its dotplot is strongly right-skewed with one outlier, so the sample-data condition is not met and the t-test is not appropriate.

(c) No. Each student provided both times, so the two sets of times are not independent samples; the analysis should use the 15 differences (a matched-pairs, one-sample procedure).
